concepts.title: Greetings and farewells
concepts.learningObjective: Greet someone and say goodbye, matching the time of day and region.
concepts.explanationMarkdown: **Hallo** and **Tschüss** work almost everywhere. More formal: **Guten Morgen / Guten Tag / Guten Abend** and **Auf Wiedersehen**. In the south you will hear **Grüß Gott**, in the north **Moin**.

commonMistakes.explanation: 'Nacht' is feminine, so no -n: 'Gute Nacht'. The -n in 'Guten Morgen/Tag/Abend' comes from masculine accusative.

concepts.title: du or Sie?
concepts.learningObjective: Choose between informal 'du' and formal 'Sie' in everyday situations.
concepts.explanationMarkdown: **du** = family, friends, children, students among themselves. **Sie** (always capitalized) = strangers, officials, business. Rule of thumb: adults you don't know get **Sie** until they offer **du**.

examples.en: Excuse me, can you help me?

commonMistakes.wrong: Hallo Herr Schmidt, wie geht es dir?
commonMistakes.right: Hallo Herr Schmidt, wie geht es Ihnen?
commonMistakes.explanation: With 'Herr/Frau + surname' use the formal Sie-forms.

concepts.title: Personal pronouns (nominative)
concepts.learningObjective: Use ich, du, er/sie/es, wir, ihr, sie/Sie as sentence subjects.
concepts.explanationMarkdown:
| Person | Singular | Plural |
|---|---|---|
| 1st | ich | wir |
| 2nd | du | ihr |
| 3rd | er / sie / es | sie |

Formal **Sie** (capitalized) is used for one or several people.

commonMistakes.wrong: sie können mir helfen? (to a stranger)
commonMistakes.explanation: Formal 'Sie' is always capitalized; lowercase 'sie' means 'she' or 'they'.

concepts.title: sein — to be (present)
concepts.learningObjective: Conjugate and use 'sein' to say who or what someone is.
concepts.explanationMarkdown:
**sein** is completely irregular:

| | |
|---|---|
| ich **bin** | wir **sind** |
| du **bist** | ihr **seid** |
| er/sie/es **ist** | sie/Sie **sind** |

commonMistakes.explanation: Professions after 'sein' take no article in German.

concepts.title: Regular verbs in the present tense
concepts.learningObjective: Conjugate regular verbs like wohnen, kommen, lernen in the present.
concepts.explanationMarkdown:
Stem + ending: ich **-e**, du **-st**, er/sie/es **-t**, wir **-en**, ihr **-t**, sie/Sie **-en**.

*wohnen*: ich wohn**e**, du wohn**st**, er wohn**t**, wir wohn**en**, ihr wohn**t**, sie wohn**en**.

concepts.title: Verb-second word order
concepts.learningObjective: Keep the conjugated verb in second position in statements.
concepts.explanationMarkdown:
In a German statement the conjugated verb is always the **second element** — the first can be the subject, a time phrase or anything else:

- **Ich** *lerne* heute Deutsch.
- **Heute** *lerne* ich Deutsch. (subject moves behind the verb!)

commonMistakes.explanation: The conjugated verb must stay in position 2; the subject moves after it when something else comes first.

concepts.title: W-questions
concepts.learningObjective: Ask open questions with wer, was, wo, woher, wie, wann.
concepts.explanationMarkdown:
Question word first, verb second, subject third:

- **Wo** *wohnst* du?
- **Woher** *kommen* Sie?
- **Wie** *heißt* du?

commonMistakes.explanation: Origin asks 'woher' (where from); 'wo' asks for a location.

concepts.title: Introducing yourself
concepts.learningObjective: Say your name, origin, home and occupation in connected sentences.
concepts.explanationMarkdown: The classic four: **Ich heiße** … / **Ich komme aus** … / **Ich wohne in** … / **Ich bin** … (profession, no article).

examples.de: Ich heiße Lena und komme aus Polen.
examples.en: My name is Lena and I come from Poland.

examples.de: Ich wohne jetzt in München und bin Studentin.
examples.en: I live in Munich now and am a student.

commonMistakes.explanation: 'heißen' is a full verb — no extra 'ist'.

concepts.title: Definite articles: der, die, das
concepts.learningObjective: Use the correct definite article and learn nouns together with their gender.
concepts.explanationMarkdown:
Every German noun has a gender: **der** (masculine), **die** (feminine), **das** (neuter). Plural is always **die**. Gender is mostly arbitrary — always learn *der Tisch*, never just *Tisch*.

Helpful patterns: **-ung, -heit, -keit → die**; **-chen, -lein → das**.

commonMistakes.explanation: Words in -chen are always neuter, even 'girl': das Mädchen.

concepts.title: Indefinite articles: ein, eine
concepts.learningObjective: Use ein/eine for unspecific things and know that plurals take no article.
concepts.explanationMarkdown: **ein** (der/das words), **eine** (die words). There is no plural of 'ein': *Das sind Bücher.*

commonMistakes.explanation: 'ein/eine' has no plural form — plural indefinite nouns stand alone.

concepts.title: Common plural forms
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize and form the most frequent plural patterns.
concepts.explanationMarkdown: Main patterns: **-e** (Tisch → Tische), **-(e)n** (Lampe → Lampen), **-er** + umlaut (Kind → Kinder), **-s** (Auto → Autos), umlaut only (Apfel → Äpfel). Learn the plural with each noun.

examples.de: Zwei Tische, drei Lampen, vier Kinder.
examples.en: Two tables, three lamps, four children.

commonMistakes.explanation: -s plurals are rare (mostly loanwords); Kind takes -er.

concepts.title: haben — to have (present)
concepts.learningObjective: Conjugate 'haben' and use it to talk about possessions.
concepts.explanationMarkdown:
| | |
|---|---|
| ich **habe** | wir **haben** |
| du **hast** | ihr **habt** |
| er/sie/es **hat** | sie/Sie **haben** |

Note du **hast** and er **hat** lose the -b-.

commonMistakes.explanation: 'haben' is irregular in du/er forms: du hast, er hat.

concepts.title: Accusative case (introduction)
concepts.learningObjective: Mark the direct object: der → den, ein → einen (masculine only).
concepts.explanationMarkdown:
The direct object stands in the **Akkusativ**. Only masculine articles change:

| | Nominativ | Akkusativ |
|---|---|---|
| m | der / ein | **den / einen** |
| f | die / eine | die / eine |
| n | das / ein | das / ein |

commonMistakes.explanation: Masculine direct objects take -en: einen Hund.

concepts.title: Negation: nicht and kein
concepts.learningObjective: Negate verbs and adjectives with 'nicht' and nouns with 'kein/keine'.
concepts.explanationMarkdown: **kein/keine** negates nouns with ein or no article: *Ich habe **kein** Auto.* **nicht** negates everything else: *Ich komme **nicht**.* / *Das ist **nicht** teuer.*

examples.en: That is not a good idea.

commonMistakes.explanation: Nouns with ein/no article are negated with kein, not nicht.

concepts.title: Yes/no questions
concepts.learningObjective: Form questions by putting the verb first; answer with ja, nein or doch.
concepts.explanationMarkdown: Verb first, subject second: *Kommst du mit?* — **Ja./Nein.** After a negative question, **doch** contradicts: *Hast du kein Geld?* — *Doch!* (Yes, I do!)

examples.en: Do you live in Berlin? — Yes.
Don't you have time? — Yes, I do!

commonMistakes.explanation: Yes/no questions start with the conjugated verb (rising intonation alone is colloquial).
